meta.notes: [bulk-tag pass: added `vault-002` tag to 51 questions] [vault batch 1: 16 balanced-length scenario rewrites] [vault batch 2: 8 balanced rewrites — all recall cleared]

questions.question: A fintech platform stores database passwords, API keys, and TLS private keys scattered across config files, environment variables, and developer laptops. Audit trails are nonexistent and rotation is manual. They want centralised storage, fine-grained access control, leasing, and tamper-evident audit logs for sensitive material. Which problem does the product solve?
options: Acts as a high-throughput cache for application configuration that is read often but rarely changed by the platform team
Centralises sensitive material with policy-based access, short-lived dynamic credentials, leasing, and an append-only audit log of every read
Replaces TLS certificate authorities with a managed root chain that signs end-entity certificates for browser-facing endpoints
Provides a queue-based message bus that routes credential-rotation events between microservices in a fan-out pattern
questions.explanation: Vault solves secrets sprawl: credentials scattered in config files, environment variables, wikis, and code repositories. It centralizes secrets with audit logging, dynamic secrets, fine-grained access control, automatic rotation, and encryption as a service. code, and environment variables

questions.question: Which Vault secrets engine generates real AWS IAM credentials with a configurable TTL that are automatically revoked on expiry?
options: Transit secrets engine
AWS secrets engine (dynamic credentials)
KV v2 secrets engine
Cubbyhole secrets engine
questions.explanation: The AWS secrets engine generates dynamic IAM access keys on demand with a TTL. Vault creates the IAM credentials, hands them to the application, and automatically deletes them when the lease expires. Each application gets unique credentials — no shared long-lived keys.

questions.question: An application needs to authenticate to Vault without human interaction. Which auth method is specifically designed for machine-to-Vault authentication?
options: LDAP auth method
Userpass auth method
AppRole auth method
GitHub auth method
questions.explanation: AppRole is designed for automated pipelines and applications. It uses a role_id (non-sensitive, can be embedded in the app) and a secret_id (sensitive, delivered separately at deploy time). This separation enforces security even in automated environments.

questions.question: After any successful authentication against Vault (userpass, AppRole, AWS IAM, Kubernetes service account, OIDC, …) the client receives the same kind of object that carries TTL, policies, accessor, and metadata, and is presented on later API calls. Which object is returned?
options: A short-lived signed JWT bearing the user's external identity claims, validated locally by each Vault node without server lookup
A session cookie scoped to the auth method that mounted the path, kept only in the client's in-memory keyring
A token with TTL, policies, accessor, and metadata that the client presents in subsequent requests until revocation or expiry
A wrapped response handle that must be unwrapped exactly once before the actual credentials become usable to the workload
questions.explanation: All Vault auth methods (AppRole, LDAP, Kubernetes, AWS, etc.) return a Vault token after successful authentication. The token has attached policies, a TTL, and an accessor. It is the core identity mechanism used for all subsequent API calls.

questions.question: A platform team writes a policy attached to an app role. Inside the policy they declare which actions the holder may perform on each path. The set of allowed actions is fixed by Vault. Which set lists capabilities a policy can grant on a path?
options: create, read, update, delete, list, sudo, deny
get, post, put, patch, delete, head, options
select, insert, update, delete, execute, grant, revoke
allow, deny, audit, broadcast, suppress, escalate, override
questions.explanation: Vault policy capabilities: create (write new), read, update (overwrite existing), delete, list (enumerate keys), sudo (root-restricted operations), deny (explicit deny overrides any allow). Policies are written in HCL or JSON and assigned to tokens at authentication time.

questions.question: A team is choosing between two flavours of the static-secrets engine. One stores only the current value of each key. The other adds versioning, soft-delete, and metadata. What is the principal difference?
options: The newer flavour persists data on Raft while the older flavour writes to the file backend, the only choice for production deployments
The newer flavour adds per-key versioning with configurable max-versions, soft-delete + undelete, and per-key metadata; the older flavour stores only the latest value
The older flavour returns secrets in JSON only, while the newer flavour adds a Protobuf wire format negotiated at request time for compactness
Audit logging is only available on the newer flavour, with the older flavour requiring an external syslog forwarder for compliance
questions.explanation: KV v2 is versioned: writing a new value keeps the old versions (configurable max). Soft-delete marks a version deleted but allows recovery. Destroy permanently removes a version. KV v1 silently overwrites data with no way to recover previous values. Use KV v2 for production. v1 overwrites data with no recovery

questions.question: A microservice requests a database credential. Instead of being handed a long-lived password from a config file, it receives a freshly generated username + password whose lifetime is bound to a lease and which Vault will revoke when the lease expires. What is this called, and what is its principal advantage?
options: Wrapping — Vault returns a one-time handle that the workload unwraps to obtain a pre-generated long-lived password from the operator
Dynamic secret — Vault generates a short-lived credential on demand, leases it, and revokes it on expiry, eliminating shared long-lived passwords from the blast radius of a leak
Response signing — Vault attaches a JWT to the secret so callers can verify provenance, but the credential itself is rotated by an external job
Static rotation — Vault stores the password unchanged and rotates it on a fixed schedule, notifying clients via a webhook ahead of the change
questions.explanation: Dynamic secrets are generated on-demand (real database users, AWS IAM keys) with a TTL. They auto-revoke when the lease expires. Key advantages: short-lived (reduces exposure window), unique per application (breach isolation), no manual rotation needed. The AWS and Database secrets engines are primary examples. each request gets unique credentials, no shared long-lived secrets

questions.question: A Vault lease is about to expire. The application calls vault lease renew. What happens if the renewal would exceed the secret's max_lease_ttl?
options: Vault grants a renewal up to the max_lease_ttl ceiling.
Vault revokes the secret immediately
Vault converts the lease to a non-expiring permanent secret
Vault allows the renewal and silently extends max_lease_ttl
questions.explanation: max_lease_ttl is a hard ceiling. Vault will renew the lease but only up to the max_lease_ttl — it cannot be renewed beyond it. Once max_lease_ttl is reached, the application must request a new secret (which creates new credentials). This design prevents indefinitely long-lived secrets. then the secret must be re-requested

questions.question: In AppRole authentication, which component is considered NON-sensitive and can be safely embedded in application code or configuration?
options: The wrapped response token
The role_id
The secret_id
The Vault token
questions.explanation: The role_id is analogous to a username — it identifies the role but doesn't grant access by itself. It can be embedded in application config. The secret_id is sensitive (like a password) and must be delivered separately, ideally at deploy time via response wrapping or a secure channel.

questions.question: An application needs to encrypt sensitive data before storing it in a database but should NOT store the encryption keys itself. Which Vault secrets engine solves this?
options: PKI secrets engine
Transit secrets engine (encryption-as-a-service)
Database secrets engine
KV v2 secrets engine
questions.explanation: The Transit secrets engine provides encryption-as-a-service. The application sends plaintext to Vault, receives ciphertext back. Vault manages the encryption keys and never exposes them. The application stores only ciphertext. Key rotation is supported — Vault can rewrap existing ciphertext with a newer key version.

questions.question: A company wants to eliminate long-lived TLS certificates (valid 1-2 years). Which Vault secrets engine enables issuing short-lived certificates on demand?
options: KV v2 secrets engine
Transit secrets engine
PKI secrets engine
SSH secrets engine
questions.explanation: The PKI secrets engine acts as an internal Certificate Authority. It issues X.509 certificates with configurable TTLs — from hours to days instead of years. Services request certificates at startup, certificates expire naturally. This eliminates manual certificate rotation and reduces the blast radius of compromised certificates.

questions.question: A developer runs vault read database/creds/my-role and gets a username and password. What happens to those credentials when the Vault lease expires?
options: The credentials are archived in the KV store
Vault sends a notification to the application to stop using them
The credentials remain valid indefinitely — Vault only tracks them internally
Vault connects to the database and drops the created user, revoking access
questions.explanation: The Database secrets engine creates real database users with the granted TTL. When the lease expires (or is explicitly revoked), Vault uses its stored connection credentials to connect to the database and execute the DROP USER statement. This makes revocation automatic and immediate.

questions.question: Which Vault component runs as a client-side daemon, handles automatic authentication, and writes secrets to local files for applications to consume?
options: Vault Sentinel
Vault Agent
Vault Server
Vault Proxy
questions.explanation: Vault Agent is a client daemon that handles auto-auth (AppRole, Kubernetes, AWS), automatically renews tokens and leases, and uses template rendering to write secrets to config files. Applications can read secrets from files without needing the Vault SDK, and Vault Agent handles all TTL management.

questions.question: A team uses response wrapping to deliver an AppRole secret_id to a new service. When the service goes to unwrap the token, it gets an error saying the token has already been used. What does this indicate?
options: Someone intercepted and unwrapped the token before the intended recipient
The service used the wrong Vault address
The Vault server restarted and cleared wrapping tokens
The wrapping token expired due to clock skew
questions.explanation: Response wrapping creates a single-use token. If the intended recipient gets an error that the wrapping token was already used, it means someone else (an interceptor) already unwrapped it. This is a key security feature: tampering becomes detectable. The team should investigate the delivery pipeline and revoke any secrets that may have been exposed.

questions.question: A security-conscious operator configures multiple audit devices on a Vault cluster: file, syslog, and a remote socket. During a partial outage every audit device fails to write simultaneously. What does Vault do with in-flight requests?
options: Continues operating normally and queues audit records in memory for replay once any device recovers, accepting bounded loss on crash
Switches to a hot-standby node that has independent audit devices, transparently retrying the request without affecting the client
Blocks all requests until at least one audit device acknowledges the write, so no operation proceeds without a durable audit record
Falls back to writing a degraded audit summary on the storage backend, marking each entry with a flag indicating reduced fidelity
questions.explanation: Vault prioritizes audit integrity over availability. If all enabled audit devices fail to write, Vault blocks all operations. This is by design — it prevents operating in an unaudited state. For HA environments, configure multiple audit devices (file + syslog) so a single failure doesn't halt operations.

questions.question: A Vault server starts and is in 'sealed' state. What must happen before it can serve any requests?
options: The root token must be re-created using vault operator init
The server must be registered with the license server
Sufficient unseal key shares must be provided to reconstruct the master key
The admin must restart the Vault service with a special flag
questions.explanation: Vault uses Shamir's Secret Sharing to split the master key. Unsealing requires providing enough key shares (quorum) to reconstruct the master key and decrypt Vault's storage. By default: 5 key shares with threshold 3. Auto-unseal (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault) automates this for production HA deployments.

questions.question: In a Vault HA cluster, a client sends a request to a standby node. What does the standby node do?
options: Promotes itself to active and processes the request
Rejects the request with a 503 error
Processes the request locally using its cached state
Forwards the request to the active node transparently
questions.explanation: In Vault HA, only one node is active at a time. Standby nodes forward requests to the active node transparently. From the client's perspective, the request succeeds regardless of which node it hits. When the active node fails, a standby is promoted to active (typically within seconds).

questions.question: A team is choosing the storage backend for a production Vault cluster. They want minimal moving parts, no external dependencies, native HA, and snapshot/restore tooling. Which advantage favours the embedded Raft option over an external consensus store?
options: Raft supports more secrets engines and auth methods than other backends, because plugins consult the backend driver to enumerate supported features
Raft removes the operational burden of running a separate consensus cluster — HA + replication are built into Vault itself, with snapshot/restore as a first-class operator command
Raft writes plaintext data and Vault encrypts at the application layer, where other backends store ciphertext that must be decrypted on read
Raft is the only backend that supports performance + disaster-recovery replication across regions, which other backends gate behind a paid tier
questions.explanation: Vault Raft integrated storage (introduced in Vault 1.4) eliminates the need for Consul or another external storage backend. Vault manages its own consensus and replication using the Raft algorithm. This simplifies deployment, reduces operational overhead, and is the recommended storage backend for new Vault deployments. Vault manages its own cluster storage

questions.question: A user authenticates to Vault via LDAP and also via GitHub. How does Vault's identity system track this as the same person?
options: Only the most recently used auth method is active at a time
An Entity is created with Aliases for each auth method.
The user must manually link their accounts in the Vault UI
Vault cannot correlate logins across different auth methods
questions.explanation: Vault Identity creates an Entity that represents a unique user or service. Each auth method login that matches creates an Alias linked to that entity. Both the LDAP alias and GitHub alias resolve to the same entity, so policies assigned to the entity apply regardless of which auth method was used. both logins resolve to the same entity and policies

questions.question: Vault Namespaces is a feature that allows multi-tenant deployments within a single cluster. Which Vault edition includes Namespaces?
options: Vault Enterprise only
Vault OSS (open-source)
Vault Community Edition
All Vault editions including the free tier
questions.explanation: Vault Namespaces is an Enterprise-only feature. It creates fully isolated Vault environments within a single cluster — each namespace has its own auth methods, secrets engines, policies, and tokens. This enables Vault-as-a-Service use cases where teams manage their own isolated Vault namespace.

questions.question: A pod running in a managed cluster needs to read database credentials from Vault. It has no pre-provisioned token or static API key — only its service-account JWT projected into the filesystem. Which auth method lets it authenticate using that JWT?
options: AppRole — the pod posts a role_id + secret_id retrieved from a sidecar that itself has long-lived credentials baked into the image
Kubernetes auth method — Vault validates the projected service-account JWT against the cluster's TokenReview API and issues a Vault token bound to a role
TLS certificate auth — the cluster issues each pod a client certificate at admission time and Vault matches it against an allow-list
AWS IAM auth — kubelet exchanges the pod identity for an AWS STS token that Vault then verifies against AWS for authentication
questions.explanation: The Kubernetes auth method validates the pod's ServiceAccount JWT token (mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token) with the Kubernetes TokenReview API. No pre-provisioned credentials are needed — the pod's identity is proven by Kubernetes itself. Vault binds roles to specific ServiceAccount names and namespaces.

questions.question: An administrator is scripting Vault setup. All auth method tuning (enabling, disabling, configuring roles for userpass, ldap, kubernetes, aws, …) must be POSTed to a consistent URL prefix. Which path prefix does Vault use for auth method configuration?
options: sys/mounts/auth/
auth/v1/methods/
sys/auth/
config/authn/
questions.explanation: Auth methods are mounted under the auth/ path prefix. For example: auth/approle/, auth/kubernetes/, auth/ldap/. The sys/ path prefix is for Vault system operations (mounting, sealing, audit, policy management). Secrets engines are mounted at their configured paths (e.g., secret/, aws/, database/).

questions.question: A high-throughput application creates thousands of Vault tokens per second. Which token type is optimized for this scenario and why?
options: Orphan tokens — they don't need parent token management
Batch tokens — they're lightweight, not stored in Vault,.
Root tokens — they bypass storage overhead
Service tokens — they're more secure for high-volume workloads
questions.explanation: Batch tokens are encoded entirely in the token string and not stored in Vault's storage backend. This makes them extremely lightweight — no storage write per token creation. They cannot be renewed and have no children, but for short-lived, high-volume use cases (Lambda functions, CI/CD jobs) they are far more efficient than service tokens. and faster to create

questions.question: Which Vault secrets engine is automatically mounted, scoped exclusively to the current token, and used internally for response wrapping?
options: Identity secrets engine
KV v1 engine at secret/
Cubbyhole secrets engine
System secrets engine at sys/
questions.explanation: The Cubbyhole secrets engine is always mounted at cubbyhole/ and is private to each token — no other token can access another token's cubbyhole. Response wrapping stores the wrapped secret in the cubbyhole of a single-use wrapping token. When the wrapping token expires, its cubbyhole (and the wrapped secret) is also destroyed.

questions.question: An operator needs to revoke a specific token without knowing the token's actual value. Which Vault concept allows this?
options: Token accessor
Token alias
Token display name
Token entity ID
questions.explanation: Every Vault token has an accessor — an opaque reference that allows administrative operations (lookup, revoke) without needing the token itself. Audit logs store the accessor, not the token. An operator can run vault token revoke -accessor <accessor> to revoke a specific token identified from audit logs.

questions.question: A policy attached to a token reads: `path "secret/data/app/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }`. The token attempts `vault kv get secret/data/app/db`. Vault allows it. The same token then tries `vault kv put secret/data/app/db @creds.json`. What happens to the write?
options: Allowed — the wildcard glob covers all verbs against any path matching the prefix, including writes, until an explicit deny rule fires
Allowed but degraded — the write succeeds and is stored under a quarantine flag pending out-of-band approval by a policy reviewer
Denied — the policy grants only the read capability on that prefix, and a write requires explicit create or update capability
Denied with a token revocation — Vault treats the attempted write as a privilege escalation and invalidates the token immediately
questions.explanation: The policy grants only 'read' capability on the path. Writing (vault kv put) requires 'create' or 'update' capability. Listing requires 'list' capability on the parent path. The policy explicitly restricts writes, so vault kv put would be denied. Note: list also requires listing the path secret/metadata/app/ for KV v2.

questions.question: On a brand-new Vault server with no data, an operator runs a single command that generates the root key, splits it into shares with a configurable threshold, and prints an initial root token. The command can only succeed once on a given cluster. Which operator command is it?
options: `vault operator init` — bootstraps a fresh cluster, returns the unseal/recovery key shares and the initial root token, and is rejected on any already-initialised cluster
`vault operator unseal` — accepts key shares one at a time until threshold is reached, then transitions the node from sealed to unsealed
`vault operator generate-root` — uses a quorum of existing key shares to mint a new root token for break-glass operations on a running cluster
`vault operator rekey` — generates fresh unseal key shares from a quorum of existing shares without invalidating the underlying root key
questions.explanation: vault operator init is run exactly once on a new Vault cluster. It generates the Shamir key shares (unseal keys) and an initial root token. The unseal keys must be securely distributed to key holders immediately. The root token should be used minimally to bootstrap initial configuration, then revoked. generating unseal keys and a root token — run ONCE on a brand new cluster

questions.question: A team wants to create a Vault policy that allows listing secrets in secret/team-a/ but prevents reading the secret VALUES. Which capability achieves this?
options: Read capability with a condition blocking value access
List capability on the metadata path without read on the data path
Sudo capability with read disabled
Create capability on secret/team-a/
questions.explanation: In KV v2, listing secrets requires 'list' on 'secret/metadata/team-a/*'. Reading secret values requires 'read' on 'secret/data/team-a/*'. By granting list on the metadata path only (without read on data), users can see secret names but cannot read their values. This separation is a KV v2 advantage over v1.

questions.question: A regulated bank wants to avoid distributing unseal-key shares to five humans. Instead, on each restart Vault should unseal itself by calling an external key-management service that protects the unseal key under a customer-managed CMK. Which mechanism delivers this?
options: Recovery keys — a parallel set of key shares with reduced privileges, distributed to the same operators with smaller share count
Transit auto-unseal using another Vault cluster's transit engine — works but defeats the goal because that other cluster still needs human unseal
Cloud KMS auto-unseal — Vault stores the encrypted root key on the backend and on startup calls AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or GCP KMS to decrypt it
Shamir auto-unseal — Vault performs the secret-sharing reconstruction itself in memory at boot, bypassing the operator quorum entirely
questions.explanation: Auto-unseal uses a cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS) or HSM to wrap/unwrap the Vault master key. On startup, Vault calls the KMS to decrypt the master key automatically — no human key holders needed. This is the recommended approach for HA production deployments. Transit auto-unseal (using another Vault's Transit engine) is also a valid option. Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS wrap the master key

questions.question: A dynamic database credential was issued with a 1-hour lease. After 10 minutes the operator runs `vault lease revoke <lease_id>` against it. What does Vault do to the underlying database password?
options: Marks the lease revoked in Vault but leaves the database account untouched; the credential remains valid in the DB until the engine's next periodic cleanup
Calls the database plugin to DROP or disable the dynamically created account, then deletes the lease metadata — the credential is no longer accepted by the database
Notifies the application via the lease watcher channel, expecting it to issue a fresh request before the password expires; the password itself is left in place
Rotates the credential's password but keeps the account, so any client still holding the old password is gracefully rejected without losing the user
questions.explanation: Revoking a dynamic database secret lease triggers immediate revocation: Vault uses its stored database connection to DROP the user that was created for that lease. The credentials become invalid instantly, not after the TTL expires. This is valuable for incident response when a credential may have been compromised.

questions.question: A Vault token has a TTL of 1 hour but the application needs it to remain valid for 8 hours. The token's max_ttl is 24 hours. What should the application do?
options: Create a new token by re-authenticating after each hour
Enable token immortality by setting TTL to 0
Change the token's TTL using vault token update
Call vault token renew before the TTL expires to extend it (up to max_ttl)
questions.explanation: Vault tokens with 'renewable: true' can be renewed before expiry using vault token renew (or the API equivalent). Each renewal extends the TTL by its increment, but the token cannot be renewed past max_ttl. Vault Agent automates this for applications. Setting TTL to 0 does NOT make a token immortal — it uses the system default TTL.

questions.question: An infrastructure team wants to grant engineers SSH access to ephemeral VMs without distributing long-lived SSH keys. Instead they want Vault to mint a one-time password per host that the host's PAM module validates against Vault. Which secrets engine fits?
options: The PKI engine — Vault signs short-lived X.509 certificates that openssh-server can validate via TrustedUserCAKeys, no per-host secret needed
The SSH engine in OTP mode — Vault generates a one-time password per session that the target host validates against Vault via the vault-ssh-helper PAM plugin
The TOTP engine — Vault stores per-host shared TOTP secrets and engineers compute a 6-digit code locally using their authenticator app
The KV engine combined with a sidecar — a daemon on each host polls Vault every 60 seconds for the rotating password and updates /etc/shadow
questions.explanation: The SSH secrets engine has two modes: OTP mode generates a single-use password for a specific user/host, and CA mode signs SSH public keys creating short-lived SSH certificates. Both eliminate the need to distribute and manage SSH keys manually. CA mode is preferred for scale as it doesn't require a Vault helper on each target host.

questions.question: A new client authenticates and receives a token with two policies listed: the application policy and another policy that is automatically attached. The auto-attached policy grants the bare minimum needed for the token to renew itself and look up its own info. Which policy is it?
options: The `root` policy, attached as a fallback when no other policy is specified at token creation, granting unrestricted access until tuned
The `default` policy, automatically attached to every non-root token unless explicitly excluded, granting self-renew, self-lookup, cubbyhole, and a few other safe operations
The `admin` policy, attached for the first hour of a token's life so that the application can complete bootstrap before being demoted
The `audit` policy, attached so that the token can write its own audit records to the configured audit devices for forensic replay
questions.explanation: The 'default' policy is automatically attached to every token created in Vault. It grants minimal permissions like token renewal (auth/token/renew-self), self-lookup (auth/token/lookup-self), and revocation (auth/token/revoke-self). You can add more permissions to the default policy or explicitly exclude it using token_no_default_policy in auth roles. self-lookup) — attached to ALL tokens automatically

questions.question: A Vault transit key has been rotated (now on version 3). Data was encrypted with versions 1 and 2. How does Vault handle decryption of old ciphertext?
options: Vault automatically re-encrypts all stored data with the new key on rotation
Old ciphertext can no longer be decrypted after key rotation
The application must manually specify the key version when decrypting
Vault maintains all key versions and can decrypt ciphertext from any non-deleted version
questions.explanation: Transit keys maintain all historical versions. The ciphertext format includes the key version prefix (vault:v1:..., vault:v2:...). Vault uses the correct version to decrypt. Key rotation creates a new version for new encryptions; old versions remain for decryption. Use vault write transit/keys/mykey/trim min_decryption_version=2 to remove older versions.

questions.question: A Vault HA cluster runs on integrated storage. The operator needs to take a consistent point-in-time backup of the entire data store (encrypted) that can later be restored on a fresh cluster as part of disaster recovery drills. They run a single CLI command that streams the snapshot to a local file. Which command does this?
options: `vault operator raft snapshot save backup.snap` — streams a consistent point-in-time snapshot of integrated storage to a local file; can be restored on a fresh cluster for disaster recovery
`vault audit enable file file_path=backup.snap` — exports an append-only log of every operation, which can be replayed against a new cluster to reconstruct state
`vault operator rekey -backup file=backup.snap` — exports the current unseal key shares so that a quorum can be reconstituted by a new operator team
`vault operator generate-root -dr backup.snap` — produces a recovery bundle containing the root token + policies that bootstraps a replacement node
questions.explanation: vault operator raft snapshot save creates a binary snapshot of the entire Raft storage state. This snapshot can be restored with vault operator raft snapshot restore to recover from data loss or cluster failure. It captures all Vault data: secrets, policies, auth config, and audit logs. Regular automated snapshots are a critical backup practice.

questions.question: An AppRole role is configured with secret_id_num_uses=1. What happens when a CI/CD system tries to use the same secret_id a second time?
options: Vault authenticates successfully but reduces the remaining use count to -1
Vault grants the authentication but logs a warning
Vault refreshes the secret_id automatically with a new one
Vault rejects the authentication.
questions.explanation: Setting secret_id_num_uses=1 makes the secret_id a single-use credential — after one successful authentication, it's consumed and cannot be used again. This is the recommended setting for CI/CD pipelines where each deployment should receive and consume a fresh secret_id. It prevents credential reuse if a secret_id is leaked. the secret_id is consumed after first use

questions.question: A platform engineer is installing a Vault binary on a fresh host. Before starting the service they create a file the binary reads at startup to learn its listener addresses, storage backend, telemetry, seal stanza, and cluster name. What does that file define?
options: The server configuration file — declares listener stanzas, storage backend, seal config, telemetry, cluster name, and other static startup parameters that Vault reads on launch
The policy bundle — a flattened list of every policy that should exist on the running server, applied automatically when the binary starts
The secrets-engine seed — pre-populates KV mounts with initial values so that smoke tests can succeed on the first boot of a fresh node
The audit ruleset — declares which paths must be logged and at what verbosity, replacing the runtime `audit enable` command for compliance
questions.explanation: vault.hcl configures the Vault server process: storage backend (raft, consul, dynamodb), listener (TCP address, TLS certificates), cluster_addr (for HA), api_addr, seal configuration (for auto-unseal), and telemetry. It does NOT store secrets or policies — those are managed via the API/CLI after the server starts. listener, cluster address, and seal configuration

questions.question: An administrator is exploring Vault's HTTP API. They notice that mount tuning, health, leader status, audit configuration, license info, and policy management are all reachable under one path prefix that maps to Vault's built-in system endpoint. Which path is it?
options: `internal/`
`admin/v1/`
`sys/`
`vault/system/`
questions.explanation: The sys/ path is Vault's system API. Key endpoints: sys/health (cluster health), sys/seal (seal the vault), sys/unseal (unseal), sys/mounts (manage secrets engine mounts), sys/auth (manage auth method mounts), sys/policies (manage policies), sys/audit (manage audit devices). Access to sys/ paths typically requires sudo capability.

questions.question: A Vault admin wants to provide an external team temporary read access to a specific secret, with the access token self-destructing after delivery. Which mechanism achieves this?
options: Create an IAM user for the team with read-only access
Enable public access on the secret path temporarily
Share the root token temporarily
Use response wrapping — deliver a wrapping token that can only be unwrapped once
questions.explanation: Response wrapping creates a single-use wrapping token that contains the secret. The admin delivers the wrapping token to the team. When unwrapped, the actual secret is returned and the wrapping token is consumed. If someone intercepts and unwraps it first, the team gets an error — making interception detectable. The wrapping token also has a TTL, after which it expires.

questions.question: A workload requests a token whose lifetime should NOT depend on the lifetime of any other token. When the token that issued the credential expires or is revoked, the new token must survive. To achieve this, the issuing token uses a specific flag at create time. What does that flag set?
options: Creates a token with no parent in Vault's token hierarchy — it is not revoked when its issuer is revoked, only by its own TTL, max_ttl, or explicit revocation
Marks the token as exempt from any audit log for the duration of its validity, so that high-throughput batch jobs do not flood downstream SIEMs
Allows the token to bypass policy checks on a configurable subset of paths to support break-glass operations during an incident
Causes the token's TTL to be refreshed every time a child token is created beneath it, effectively pinning the parent's lifetime to the child's
questions.explanation: Normally, revoking a parent token revokes all its child tokens. An orphan token (token_type = orphan) has no parent — it exists independently. This is important for long-running services that authenticate via AppRole: the AppRole login token is ephemeral (parent), but the service shouldn't lose access just because the login token expired. Orphan tokens persist until their own TTL expires or they're explicitly revoked. it survives independently of the creating token's lifecycle

questions.question: A Vault audit log shows a request with HMAC-ed token value. Why are token values HMACed in audit logs?
options: To compress the logs for storage efficiency
To prevent the actual token from being readable in logs.
To allow log replay for debugging purposes
To encrypt all audit log entries for compliance
questions.explanation: Vault HMACs sensitive values (tokens, secrets) in audit logs using a salt. The HMAC allows correlation (same token = same HMAC across all log entries) without exposing the actual token value. An attacker who obtains audit logs cannot extract usable tokens. Administrators use accessors (not HMACs) for operational token management. protecting against log-based token theft while still allowing correlation

questions.question: On a KV-v2 mount, an operator runs `vault kv delete secret/app/db` then later runs `vault kv destroy -versions=3 secret/app/db`. The first command leaves the data recoverable; the second does not. What is the difference?
options: The first removes the latest version from the listing while keeping all earlier versions readable; the second permanently deletes the listing entry for every prior version
Both commands permanently remove data; the difference is purely that the second writes an audit record at higher verbosity, with no behavioural distinction
The first marks specific versions as soft-deleted (recoverable via `vault kv undelete`); the second permanently wipes the underlying data for the specified versions and is irreversible
The first removes only the policy that allows reads, leaving data intact; the second wipes the data and the policy, requiring re-grant before any further reads
questions.explanation: KV v2 soft-delete (vault kv delete): marks the version as deleted, but the data remains recoverable with vault kv undelete. Destroy (vault kv destroy): permanently removes the version data — irreversible. The metadata (version history) still shows the version existed, but the secret data is gone. Use destroy for secrets that must be truly purged (e.g., compromised credentials). destroy permanently removes specific version data

questions.question: An application runs in AWS EC2. Which Vault auth method allows the EC2 instance to authenticate without any pre-placed secrets?
options: LDAP auth using the EC2 hostname
TLS certificate auth using the instance's TLS certificate
AppRole with the role_id stored in user-data
AWS auth method using the EC2 instance identity document signed by AWS
questions.explanation: The AWS auth method supports EC2 authentication using the signed instance identity document (from IMDS). Vault verifies the document's signature with AWS's public certificate, confirming the identity of the EC2 instance without pre-placed credentials. Vault can bind roles to specific AMI IDs, accounts, regions, or IAM roles.

questions.question: An operator wants to force a controlled leader election on a Vault HA cluster — perhaps to drain the active node before an OS upgrade. They run a CLI command on the active node that causes it to relinquish leadership; another standby is then promoted. Which command does this?
options: Forces the current active Vault node to relinquish leadership, sealing itself and triggering an election among the standbys to promote a new active node
Drains in-flight requests on the active node and queues new ones until the operator manually promotes a standby with a `force-promote` call
Pauses replication to performance-secondary clusters so that the active node can complete maintenance without affecting downstream replicas
Disables the read-replica role on the local node and promotes it to perform an out-of-cluster restore from the latest Raft snapshot
questions.explanation: vault operator step-down forces the active Vault node to give up its leadership. A standby node then wins the leader election and becomes active. This is used for planned maintenance, rolling upgrades, or testing failover. The stepped-down node becomes a standby and remains in the cluster. triggering a failover to a standby node

questions.question: Which Vault feature allows path-based routing rules to override or deny access based on contextual information like time of day or IP address? (Enterprise)
options: Vault Sentinel / Endpoint Governing Policies (EGPs) and Role Governing Policies (RGPs)
ACL templating in policies
LDAP group-based policy assignment
Token metadata conditions
questions.explanation: Vault Enterprise includes Sentinel-based Endpoint Governing Policies (EGPs) and Role Governing Policies (RGPs). These allow complex policy logic (time-based, IP-based, MFA-required conditions) using HashiCorp Sentinel's policy-as-code framework. This goes beyond static ACL capabilities. EGPs apply to specific paths; RGPs apply to roles.

questions.question: A team stores secrets at secret/data/team-a/db. They want to enforce that only tokens with entity metadata 'team=team-a' can access this path. Which Vault ACL template feature enables this?
options: Vault cannot use token metadata for policy decisions
ACL templating with {{identity.entity.metadata.team}} in the policy path
AWS IAM condition keys in Vault policies
LDAP group binding to the secret path
questions.explanation: Vault ACL templating allows dynamic policy paths using identity metadata. A policy like path 'secret/data/{{identity.entity.metadata.team}}/*' { capabilities = ['read'] } restricts each entity to only their team's secrets path. The placeholder resolves at policy evaluation time based on the authenticated entity's metadata.

questions.question: A new operator on a fresh Vault server wants to enable the database secrets engine at a custom path so the team can mint dynamic Postgres credentials. They have access to the host but have not interacted with the API yet. What MUST happen first?
options: The server must be initialised AND unsealed, and the operator must be authenticated with a token whose policy grants the required capabilities on `sys/mounts/<path>`
The host must have a working Postgres driver installed locally, because mounts call out to the database plugin during the enable handshake
An audit device must be enabled, because mount operations are rejected on clusters where no audit device has been configured for any path
The license file must declare the database engine in the entitlements bundle, because the engine is gated behind a premium tier even in non-prod
questions.explanation: The first step is vault secrets enable -path=myengine <engine-type> (e.g., vault secrets enable -path=aws aws). This mounts the engine at the specified path. After mounting, you configure the engine (e.g., vault write aws/config/root credentials). Policies can be created before or after, but the engine must be mounted before it can be used.

questions.question: An operator runs vault token lookup and sees 'renewable: false'. What does this mean for the token lifecycle?
options: The token will never expire
The token can only be renewed by root users
The token can be renewed but the TTL won't increase
The token will expire at its TTL and cannot be extended.
questions.explanation: A non-renewable token cannot be extended with vault token renew. Once its TTL expires, it becomes invalid. The application must re-authenticate to get a new token. Batch tokens are always non-renewable by design. Some auth method roles can be configured to issue non-renewable tokens for security purposes. a new token must be obtained

questions.question: What is the vault CLI environment variable used to set the Vault server address so you don't have to pass -address on every command?
options: VAULT_ENDPOINT
VAULT_URL
VAULT_ADDR
VAULT_HOST
questions.explanation: VAULT_ADDR sets the default Vault server address (e.g., export VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.example.com:8200). Other important Vault environment variables: VAULT_TOKEN (default token), VAULT_NAMESPACE (namespace for Enterprise), VAULT_CACERT (CA certificate path), VAULT_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY (skip TLS verification, NOT for production).

questions.question: A company wants to ensure that even if the Vault database is stolen, stored secrets cannot be read. What protects the data at rest in Vault's storage backend?
options: TLS encryption on the Vault API listener
Vault's barrier encryption.
File system permissions on the storage directory
The storage backend's native encryption (e.g., S3 SSE)
questions.explanation: Vault's cryptographic barrier encrypts ALL data before writing to the storage backend using the master key (derived from the unseal keys). This means even if someone steals the raw storage (Consul KV, DynamoDB, Raft files), they cannot read any secrets without the master key. This is why Vault starts 'sealed' — the master key is not in memory until unsealing occurs. all data written to storage is encrypted using the master key before being stored

questions.question: A token is issued with TTL=1h and max_ttl=24h. The application renews the token roughly every 45 minutes while it is running. Which TWO statements about its lifetime are accurate? (select two)
options: Each renewal can extend the token's expiry by up to TTL=1h from the renewal moment, but never past max_ttl=24h from initial creation
Renewals reset both TTL and max_ttl, so a long-running process can keep the same token alive indefinitely with periodic renewals
After 24 hours from creation the token expires regardless of how recently it was renewed; the application must authenticate again to obtain a fresh token
The token enters a grace period after expiry during which it can still authorise reads but is rejected for any write operation against any path
questions.explanation: max_ttl is the hard cap on total lifetime from creation, regardless of renewals. As you approach max_ttl, the renewal grant shrinks (Vault returns less than the requested TTL). Renewals are NOT automatic — clients must call /auth/token/renew. Use cases like agent auto-auth handle that on the client side.
